title: Forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11)
hookLine: hungry and alone, he's offered bread, spectacle and power, and says no three times

lines: THE TEMPTER COMES AT THE END.
cards: Hunger changes how a person thinks. Not snack hunger. Skip two meals and everything gets louder, and judgment gets worse.
Now stretch that much further. Right after the voice at the river, Matthew says, the Spirit leads Jesus up into the wilderness. He fasts forty days and forty nights.
And then, with a kind of dry understatement, the text says he was hungry. That's when the tempter comes. Not at the start, when he's strong.
At the end, when he's weakest.

teach.h: IF THOU BE THE SON OF GOD.
teach.b: The first words, in the King James Bible: "If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread." If. The voice at the river just said, this is my beloved Son.
The first temptation goes straight for that: prove it. The answer: "It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God."
Then a pinnacle of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. A spectacle. Make them believe.
"It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Then a high mountain, and all the kingdoms of the world, offered for one act of worship. Power, the fast way.
"Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve."
And all three answers come from one book, Deuteronomy, from the chapters where Moses remembers Israel's forty years in the wilderness, when they were hungry and tested too.
Forty years for a people, forty days for one man, answering with the words his people learned in the desert.
Churches that keep Lent count forty days before Easter in memory of these forty, fasting a little and saying no to something.

This week began in the temple with Simeon's Nunc dimittis and Anna's thanks. Then the magi, a family fleeing to Egypt, a boy asking questions, a wild man by the river, the baptism, and now the desert. Beloved first.

how: Many churches keep Lent, the forty days before Easter, in memory of these forty days, with fasting, prayer and giving; the temptation story is often read on the first Sunday of Lent. Practices range from giving up a food or habit to fasting on set days.

o: a punishment sent for breaking God's law
a test that offers a shortcut to do wrong
a vision that shows the future

games.q: three offers, three answers — tap the pairs.
p: thou shalt not tempt the Lord

s: the tempter came at the start of the forty days
Matthew says he came afterward, when Jesus was hungry.
all three of Jesus's answers come from Deuteronomy
from the chapters about Israel's forty years in the wilderness.
Lent's forty days echo this story
churches that keep Lent count forty days before Easter.

games.q: you've fasted forty days. you're starving. a voice says: if you're the Son of God, turn these stones into bread. what do you do?
o: make the bread. you're hungry, and it proves the point.
answer with scripture: not by bread alone.
games.why: he answers: it is written, man shall not live by bread alone. he refuses to prove what the voice at the river already said.

practice: Think of one small temptation that finds you on an ordinary day, not the biggest one: the extra hour on the phone, the sharp reply, the thing you buy to feel better, the shortcut.
Picture the moment it usually arrives, when you're tired or hungry or bored, and picture yourself saying no to it, once, calmly. If you pray, you can ask for strength for that moment.

wordCard.voice: Temptation. Three offers of bread, spectacle and power, tested after forty days alone in the wilderness. This week's words: Nunc dimittis, the magi, the Holy Innocents, the boy among the doctors, metanoia, baptism.

orig.note: Greek: testing, trial, temptation. The same word is in the Lord's Prayer's line: lead us not into temptation.

carryVoice: Your line: not by bread alone. Next week, the road through Galilee fills up with fishermen. That's week seven.
